## Abstract

Enhancing pyroelectric performance is essential for advancing thermal sensing and energy-

harvesting applications. This study presents an effective strategy to achieve highly enhanced

pyroelectricity in a flexible polyvinylidene fluoride/muscovite bimorph. Unlike conventional

approaches that focus on domain-phase engineering to enhance intrinsic pyroelectric contribution,

we engineer a more dominant role for the secondary pyroelectric contribution by a stress-induced

shape change that couples to a change in the polarization via the piezoelectric effect. This

mechanism is enabled by the favorable combination of a large thermal-expansion mismatch

between the polymer (polyvinylidene fluoride) and the ceramic (muscovite), together with the

inherent mechanical compliance of mica’s flexibility, which allows interfacial thermal stresses to

efficiently generate piezoelectricity. By combining experimental characterization with finite

element modeling of the heterostructure’s temperature-dependent curvature, interfacial thermal

stress is identified as the dominant contributor to the large effects. Direct pyroelectric

measurements reveal a highly enhanced pyroelectric coefficient  -359 µC/m2K, more than an

order of magnitude greater than that of single-layer polyvinylidene fluoride, highlighting its

potential for applications in flexible electronics, thermal sensors, and energy harvesting systems.

minimized to ensure measurement accuracy9. However, our work represents a conceptual

departure from the conventional paradigm: instead of suppressing thermal expansion mismatch,

we intentionally engineer the device structure to maximize it, transforming this "parasitic" effect

composed of two materials with different CTEs. When heated or cooled, these materials expand

or contract at unequal rates, generating mechanical stress at their interface that drives thermal

actuation (strain or bending). Therefore, by incorporating a polar material into the bimorph,

thermal energy not only triggers the πprimary but also induces the πsecondary through thermally induced

stress, potentially amplifying the material’s ability to convert thermal energy of temperature

oscillations into electrical energy. The flexible polar system used in this study is PVDF, a flexible

polymer known for its ferroelectric, piezoelectric, and pyroelectric properties. Its mechanical

flexibility, relatively low dielectric constant11, and stability under ambient conditions make it an

ideal candidate for this application.

In previous studies on flexible nanogenerators based on PVDF-based heterostructures,

researchers have extensively investigated their piezoelectric and pyroelectric effects10, 12, 13. For

example, the piezoelectric and pyroelectric properties of a PVDF/thermoplastic polyurethane

(TPU) heterostructure were investigated for wearable electronics10. However, since TPU has a

CTE similar to that of PVDF, πsecondary was negligible due to the lack of significant thermal-

expansion mismatch (Δα). While extensive efforts have been made to enhance piezoelectric and

pyroelectric response of PVDF-based heterostructures, there is considerably less understanding of

how large thermal-interfacial stresses can be leveraged to control and enhance the πsecondary.

Therefore, to achieve a larger Δα between PVDF and the substrate, in this case mica, a two-

dimensional layered ceramic was selected as an optimal candidate. It offers exceptional

mechanical flexibility and thermal stability, making it well-suited for forming thermal bimorphs

and efficiently accommodating thermally induced stresses14, 15. Here, we developed a PVDF/mica

bimorph structure, where the combination of polymer (PVDF) and ceramic (mica) maximizes the

Δα, inducing significant interfacial stress that enhances the πsecondary via the piezoelectric response.

Through a combination of structural optimization, theoretical modeling, and experimental

validation, π  -359 µC/m2K was achieved in the PVDF/mica system, exceeding that of a single-

layer PVDF (-29 µC/m2K) by over an order of magnitude. This study paves the way for using an

interface-coupling mechanism to address the current bottleneck in optimizing the π and expanding

potential applications in thermal-energy harvesting and temperature sensing.

To investigate the structural, piezoelectric, and optical properties of PVDF, mica, and their

heterostructures (fabrication details in the Methods; Supplementary Fig. S1A), a combination of

analytical techniques was employed (Methods). The crystalline phases of PVDF were analyzed

using Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy. PVDF can exist

in different crystalline forms (α, β, γ, and δ), determined by variations in molecular-chain

arrangement16. Among these, the α (non-polar) and β (polar) phases dominate at room temperature.

The β-phase is particularly desirable for pyroelectric and piezoelectric applications due to its

aligned dipole structure, leading to enhanced spontaneous polarization and results in a higher

pyroelectric response. In contrast, the non-polar α phase has randomly oriented dipoles, resulting

in a much weaker π. To synthesize PVDF with a higher β-phase proportion, the fabrication process

and parameters can be optimized and refined based on the FTIR and Raman spectroscopy results,

which reveal the relative fractions of the α and β phases in the fabricated PVDF.

First, the FTIR spectrum (Fig. 1B, Method) exhibits various absorption valleys attributed

to its crystalline phases. Since different PVDF phases exhibit distinct infrared absorption features,

both α and β phases were identified16. Furthermore, the Raman spectroscopy was further employed

as a more precise method for quantifying the β-phase fraction17. The number of Raman-active

modes is determined by the vibrations of linear (-CH2-CF2-)n PVDF molecular chains (Fig. 1C,

inset) crystallized in either the α phase with a trans–gauche (TGTG′) conformation or the β phase

with an all-trans (TTTT) conformation. Consistent with the FTIR results, the Raman spectrum

lacks the signature γ-phase peak typically observed around 811-814 cm-1. Consequently, the

material was modeled as a binary system of α and β phases , which were identified by the CH2

group rocking vibrations characteristic of the α phase and the β phase, respectively (Fig. 1C). By

analyzing these peaks, the β-phase portion was quantified, enabling ready process optimization.

Therefore, the fabrication process was refined by adjusting key parameters, including processing

temperature and PVDF concentration in solution (details of the optimization process are provided,

Supplementary Fig. S1). Following optimization, the maximum β-phase proportion achieved was

approximately 61% (supplementary Fig. S1B and S1C).

The remaining ≈39% corresponds to the α phase, which is nonpolar and does not

contribute to the piezoelectric or pyroelectric response. The functional dominance of the β phase

was further experimentally verified by piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM). PFM was further

utilized to probe the piezoelectric response and investigate the domain structure of the fabricated

heterostructure. In the PFM measurements (Methods, and Supplementary Fig. S2.), a thin indium-

tin oxide (In2O3:SnO2=90:10, ITO) layer was placed between the PVDF and mica, serving as a

conductive-bottom electrode that accommodates thermal mismatch while remaining inherently

non-pyroelectric due to its centrosymmetric crystal structure, ensuring no additional signal

generation. PFM amplitude measurements were conducted under sweeping AC voltages from 1 V

to 5 V (Fig. 1D). The amplitude exhibited a linear dependence on the applied voltage, confirming

the intrinsic piezoelectric nature of the heterostructure. By comparing the slope of this amplitude-

voltage curve with that of a standard BiFeO3 (BFO) reference (d33 ≈ 70 pm/V), we determined the

effective piezoelectric coefficient (d33) of the PVDF/mica heterostructure to be approximately 29

pm/V. This value is consistent with reported literature values for high-quality PVDF 11. To

investigate the polar domain structure, PFM amplitude and phase images (Supplementary Note.

S2) were acquired in both out-of-plane and in-plane directions. As the β phase of PVDF is polar,

it contributes to the detectable out-of-plane piezoresponse, while the non-polar α phase yields no

signal. Furthermore, the macroscopic piezoelectric response was characterized using a single-

electrode-based transparent flexible nanogenerator technique (Methods)18.

The measured average open-circuit voltages for the bending process (Fig. 1E) were +2.1

V (convex, tensile) and -1.8 V (flat, release), indicating that tensile stress induces a positive output,

while the returning-to-flat process (which involves compressive stress) yields a negative output.

The polarity reversal and asymmetric signal output confirm that interfacial stress induced by

bending leads to opposite charge generation, confirming the piezoelectric behavior of the

heterostructure. Moreover, the device maintained a highly stable output voltage over 1,000

mechanical bending cycles without observable degradation, indicating a good interfacial adhesion

of the bilayer. The optical transmittance was obtained by using the UV-Vis spectroscopy

(Methods) , the wide band gaps of mica (5.0 eV), ITO (4.0 eV), and PVDF ( 6.0 eV) ensure high

optical transparency (> 75%) in the visible range (400-700 nm), minimizing parasitic optical

absorption and enhancing signal stability. This feature is beneficial for thermal-sensing

applications, as it reduces interference from ambient visible light (Fig. 1F).

The thermal properties of the PVDF/muscovite heterostructures, including the CTE of

PVDF and mica, and the bending curvature induced by thermal stress, were studied as

schematically illustrated in Fig. 2A. Temperature-dependent X-ray diffraction and Raman

spectroscopy were utilized to evaluate the CTE (Methods and Supplementary Fig. S3). Reciprocal

space mapping of mica (Fig. 2B and Supplementary Fig. S3) using the 048 diffraction condition

revealed an increase in lattice parameter from 6.86 Å at 30 °C to 6.88 Å at 230 °C, corresponding

to calculated in-plane and out-of-plane CTEs of ≈ 7.9 ppm/K and ≈ 15.7 ppm/K, respectively. The

in-plane thermal expansion is identified as the governing factor in the bimorph bending mechanism.

For PVDF (Fig. 2C), which is considered to exhibit isotropic thermal expansion, the CTE was

determined to be  120 ppm/K by analyzing the temperature-dependent Raman shift of the CH2

wagging vibration mode at 840 cm-1. With increasing temperature, the Raman peak shifted toward

lower wavenumbers from 841.7 cm-1 at 25 °C to 841.1 cm-1 at 74 °C. These experimental results

confirm a significant difference in CTEs between PVDF and mica. As PVDF tends to expand more

significantly than mica, this mismatch effectively produces in-plane compressive stresses within

the PVDF and tensile stresses in the mica.

We further analyzed the deformation behavior induced by thermal stress, using the

PVDF/mica heterostructure as a thermally actuated device for heating tests. The sample was heated

from room temperature to 100°C in a preheated oven, and its deformation was recorded using

camera-based imaging (Methods and Supplementary Fig. S4A). The evolution of bending

curvature over time was analyzed (Fig. 2D). Initially flat, the heterostructure exhibited a rapid

increase in curvature with a rise time < 1 s, followed by a slower recovery to its original state > 5

s. A positive correlation between curvature and temperature was observed, indicating that

differential thermal expansion between the layers drives the bending deformation. To optimize the

thermal-actuation performance, the mica thickness was systematically varied while maintaining

the optimized β-phase-rich PVDF at a fixed thickness of 20 µm. The goal was to identify the mica

thickness that yields the largest bending curvature in response to temperature variations. Thinner

mica layers resulted in greater bending curvature (Fig. 2E). The optimal configuration was

identified as 20 µm PVDF paired with 20 µm mica. A thinner mica layer positions the neutral axis

of the heterostructures closer to the PVDF/mica interface, which is more effective for inducing

interfacial thermal stress. Notably, reducing the mica thickness below 20 µm presents significant

challenges for practical applications. Thinner layers are difficult to reliably exfoliate using

mechanical methods, often resulting in damage or non-uniform thickness. Furthermore, while

reducing thickness theoretically enhances the bending curvature, it significantly lowers the critical

load that the substrate can sustain. This renders the samples mechanically fragile and challenging

to handle, making them highly susceptible to fracture under bending-induced stress.

on thermal bending. Using the experimentally extracted CTEs (α1 = 120 ppm/K for PVDF, α2 =

7.9 ppm/K for mica) and mechanical properties (E1 = 3.9 GPa, E2 = 110 GPa), the calculated

curvature of the 20 µm PVDF / 20 µm mica heterostructures increased linearly with ΔT (Fig. 2F

While the Timoshenko bilayer model provides a useful baseline to estimate the thermal

bending curvature and strain (Supplementary Fig. S4C), the calculation assumes uniform strain

distribution and temperature-independent, isotropic material properties. Specifically, it neglects

the anisotropy inherent in mica (e.g., Ex ≠ Ez, αx ≠ αz) and the temperature-dependent elastic

stiffness tensors of both PVDF and mica (Tables S1-S2). To more accurately simulate the

deformation behavior under realistic thermal environments, we performed finite element method

(FEM) simulations (Supplementary Fig. S4D, Fig. S5) incorporating temperature-dependent and

anisotropic material properties (Table S2). The FEM model also accounts for thermal conductivity,

specific-heat capacity, and convective heat transfer at the exposed surfaces, enabling a more

comprehensive treatment of coupled thermomechanical behavior. The curvature values predicted

by FEM simulations (Fig. 2F, dashed line) agree well with experimental trends, confirming the

reliability of the model across the operational temperature range.

For benchmarking (Fig. 2F), the thermal-actuation performance of the PVDF/mica

heterostructures was compared with those using silver (Ag), copper (Cu), and amorphous copper

metal layers in place of PVDF. Among all configurations, PVDF/mica demonstrates the largest

bending curvature. This enhancement is attributed to the pronounced Δα: PVDF possesses a high

coefficient of thermal expansion (120 ppm/K), while metals typically range from 6-35 ppm/K and

mica remains much lower at 7.9 ppm/K. This resulting large mismatch drives strong interfacial

thermal stress, enabling enhanced thermal-actuation performance.

To investigate the role of Δα and substrate mechanical effects on the pyroelectric properties,

we conducted pyroelectric measurements using the PVDF/mica system. In addition, two reference

systems, including PVDF on sapphire and a single-layer PVDF film, were prepared to serve as

comparisons, revealing how differences in substrate stiffness and thermal-expansion behavior

impact the pyroelectric performance (Fig. 3A). Devices were fabricated with a layered structure

of 200 nm ITO / 20 µm PVDF / 200 nm ITO on mica, on commercial sapphire substrates, and as

a single-layer film, where ITO serves as both the top and bottom electrodes.

Pyroelectric measurements were conducted using the Garn-Sharp method21, 22, in which

sinusoidal temperature oscillations (ΔT(t) = T0 sin (ωt)) were induced to heat up the devices and

the resulting pyrocurrent can be expressed as:

Where A is the electrode area and ω the angular heating frequency. This expression shows that the

pyrocurrent is phase-shifted by approximately 90° relative to the temperature profile, serving as a

signature to distinguish the genuine pyroelectric response from in-phase thermal or leakage

currents for PVDF/mica, PVDF/sapphire, and single-layer PVDF (blue, green and purple curves,

left axis) were recorded (Fig. 3B). Given the thermal mass of Peltier-based measurement setup,

we evaluated the frequency dependence (Supplementary Note 6) and selected a low heating

frequency of 0.05 Hz to ensure sufficient thermal equilibration. At higher frequencies, thermal

damping occurs as the heat transfer rate limits the effective temperature oscillation amplitude

inside the sample. The PVDF/mica device exhibits the largest pyrocurrent amplitude and a clean

sinusoidal waveform with the expected 90° phase shift relative to temperature, while the

PVDF/sapphire and single-layer PVDF samples show much smaller amplitudes.

Further, to quantitatively determine the π, the amplitude of the temperature oscillations (To)

was varied, the peak of pyrocurrent amplitude was extracted, and the slope of the linear fit (πAω)

was used to calculate the π. A higher slope indicates a higher π for devices with the same electrode

area (A) and heating frequency (ω). The π determined from such measurements (Fig. 3C) were as

follows: PVDF on mica (-359 µC/m2K), PVDF on sapphire (-32 µC/m2K), and a single-layer

PVDF film (-29 µC/m2K). Among these samples, the PVDF/mica heterostructure exhibits the

highest π, achieving an enhancement of more than one order of magnitude, attributed to the

favorable combination of a large Δα and the mechanical compliance of mica. This strain, acting

through the film’s piezoelectric coefficient, contributes to a considerable πsecondary. It should be

noted that the sign of the πsecondary is the same as the πprimary, with both being negative since the d31

coefficient of PVDF is positive, and the PVDF/mica interface experiences compressive stress

under thermal stimuli, thus the resulting piezoelectric polarization change is negative.

In contrast, the PVDF/sapphire heterostructures, despite also exhibiting a large Δα, show

no significant πsecondary enhancement. We attribute this behavior to interfacial mechanical coupling.

Sapphire possesses a rigid 3D covalently/ionically bonded surface with a high Young’s modulus(

360 GPa)23, which is expected to strongly constrain interfacial deformation and limit effective

thermal stress transfer into the PVDF layer. Under such conditions, the stress-mediated

piezoelectric contribution to the total pyroelectric response is suppressed. This accounts for the

low pyroelectric response ( -32 µC/m2K) observed in our PVDF/sapphire control samples.

Conversely, while mica is also a ceramic material, its unique 2D-layered structure governed by

weak van der Waals forces; thus, we propose that this van der Waals surface acts as a mechanically

compliant interface.  The mica interface facilitates the thermal stress required for the secondary

pyroelectric effect. This behavior is consistent with an enhanced dipolar response to the induced

stress, yielding the large pyroelectric coefficient (-359 µC/m2K). Therefore, the role of mica

extends beyond providing macroscopic flexibility for actuator-related applications. The specific

interfacial compliance is a factor for amplifying the stress-induced response, a feature that

intrinsically rigid 3D crystals like sapphire lack.

In the case of the single-layer PVDF film, free thermal expansion is isotropic and does not

generate in-plane anisotropic strain, resulting in no πsecondary. Collectively, these results highlight

that only substrates which have both a large thermal-expansion-coefficient difference with the

pyroelectric layer and sufficient mechanical flexibility, such as mica, can be used to effectively

induce sufficient Δα to dramatically enhance the πsecondary in PVDF-based heterostructures.

Furthermore, the PVDF/mica heterostructures demonstrate robust thermal stability and durability

(Supplementary Note 7). The pyroelectric coefficient remained constant with the initial

temperature increased from 24°C to 65°C. Supporting this macroscopic stability, temperature-

dependent P-E loop analysis (Supplementary Fig. S7B) confirmed that the ferroelectric

polarization is fully reversible even after heating. This ensures that the intrinsic piezoelectric

coefficient remains robust without permanent degradation within the operating range. In addition

to thermal stability, the device exhibits good durability as described in Supplementary Note 8. The

device maintained stable output performance during repeated thermal cycling, although the output

voltage varied with different pre-bending states (Supplementary Fig. S8A and S8B). Moreover,

extended fatigue tests demonstrated good durability, where the device showed minimal

degradation (< 4% variation) during the first 5,000 thermal cycles (Supplementary Fig. S8C),

suggesting its potential suitability for long-term practical applications.

Finally, we compared our approach with representative CTE-driven secondary (stress-

mediated) pyroelectric mechanisms (Fig. 3D). To effectively enhance the πtotal through the πsecondary,

it is essential to understand the underlying mechanism and ensure that both the πprimary and πsecondary

are aligned in sign. These mechanisms can be broadly divided into two categories: inorganic

ferroelectric systems (bulk single crystals, epitaxial thin films) and polymer-based systems (PVDF

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

composites, liquid-crystalline elastomer (LCE) nanocomposites, macro-fiber composites (MFCs)

and PVDF/mica heterostructures).

Inorganic ferroelectrics provide the first basis for comparison. In bulk single crystals, such

as LiNbO324, πprimary dominates (negative sign, from reduced spontaneous polarization with

temperature), while πsecondary, arising from positive thermal expansion along the polar axis,

typically has the opposite sign, reducing πtotal. In epitaxial polydomain ferroelectric thin-films on

rigid oxide substrates, the film is clamped in-plane, and in-plane Δα is converted into biaxial stress.

The sign of the resulting πsecondary depends on both the polarization orientation and the relative

coefficients of thermal expansion of the film and substrate25 . For example, PbZr0.2Ti0.8O3 ( α=

5.4 ×10-6 /K) thin film on GdScO3 (110) substrate (α= 12.1 ×10-6 /K), the tensile stress leads to the

change of volume fraction of c-domain and decreases the out-of-plane polarization, which c-axis

contraction and a negative πsecondary that adds constructively to the πprimary, enhancing the πtotal by

25%-50%.

In the case of polymer-based systems, the effectiveness of the πsecondary depends on  how

the Δα is engineered, and the structural connectivity and mechanical boundary conditions that

determine whether the resulting thermally generated stress can be efficiently accommodated.

Unlike rigid epitaxial films where stress is intrinsically imposed through biaxial clamping,

polymers are mechanically compliant and therefore require specific structural designs to ensure

effective stress transfer. A common approach is embedding ferroelectric particles in a polymer

matrix (0-3 connectivity), where local Δα around discrete particles generates stress; however,

πsecondary is modest because stress is generated locally and remains spatially fragmented. Chew et

al.26 showed experimentally and via effective-medium modeling that increasing the PZT volume

fraction in PVDF from 0.2 to 0.6 raises the πtotal (-18 to -42 µC/m2K), mostly through the primary

term, with only a modest rise in the πsecondary (-6 to -11 µC/m2K). To further improve,

nanocomposites with liquid-crystalline elastomers have been reported27 , where the nematic-

isotropic transition of the LCE provides a much larger thermomechanical drive and amplifies

πsecondary, increasing the πtotal from -27 to -40.1 µC/m2K (≈ 49%). Likewise, in MFC architectures,

the πsecondary is highly tunable in both magnitude and sign, depending on fiber orientation and matrix

properties. Acosta et al. 28 demonstrated that controlling the poling direction of PbZr1–xTixO3 fiber

relative to thermal expansion anisotropy can switch πsecondary from opposing (Δαmax ∥ poling axis,

+178 µC/m2K) to aligning constructively (Δαmax ⊥ poling axis, -221 µC/m2K) with πprimary. These


<!-- Page 15 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

examples highlight the importance of structural design in controlling the interplay between πprimary

and πsecondary for practical device optimization. Complementary approaches have also shown that

morphology-driven enhancement of the piezoelectric coefficient (d33), for example through

electrospun nanofiber architectures, can indirectly amplify πsecondary, enabling absolute pyroelectric

coefficients of approximately 63 µC/m2K in PVDF-based systems29. In contrast, the PVDF/mica

bilayer (2-2 connectivity) exploits a large Δα between film and substrate together with its unique

van der Waals interactions to provide a compliant boundary condition.

Beyond comparisons of secondary-contribution mechanisms, we also evaluated the

performance of the PVDF/mica heterostructures using the voltage figure of merit (FoM = π/εr) 30,

which is defined as the change in output voltage per unit temperature change. For the PVDF/mica

heterostructures, the FoM was  32.6 µC/m2K, a substantial improvement of FoM attributed to the

combined effects of a significantly enhanced π and the intrinsically low εr of PVDF ( 11;

Supplementary Note S9). A detailed comparison with other pyroelectric materials is provided in

the Supporting Information 10.

In summary, this study demonstrates that thermally induced interfacial stress can act as a

dominant mechanism for enhancing the total pyroelectric response in flexible PVDF/mica bimorph

heterostructures through secondary contributions. This finding shifts the design paradigm beyond

conventional domain-phase engineering for tuning intrinsic pyroelectric contribution, toward a

mechanically driven strategy that exploits the large thermal expansion mismatch between


<!-- Page 17 -->


ARTICLE IN PRESS

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

dissimilar materials. The heterostructure achieves a high π of -359 μC/m2K, over an order of

magnitude greater than that of pristine PVDF (-29 μC/m2K), accompanied by a high voltage figure-

of-merit owing to the low dielectric permittivity of the PVDF. The explored frequency range (0.01-

0.05 Hz) aligns with real-world thermal fluctuations, supporting its potential for low-frequency

sensing and energy harvesting. These results provide both fundamental insight into thermal stress-

driven polarization mechanisms and a practical, scalable route for engineering high-performance

pyroelectric devices. Ultimately, this work establishes a direction for enhancing pyroelectric

susceptibility in soft materials by controlling interfacial thermal-stress engineering, opening

opportunities for next-generation flexible electronics, sensors, and energy-harvesting technologies.

## Methods

Sample Fabrication of PVDF/mica heterostructures. The integration of PVDF and mica was achieved using the tape-casting method, a scalable technique well-suited for fabricating large-area and uniform films. In this process, the PVDF solution was prepared by dissolving PVDF powder in Dimethylacetamide (DMAC) under continuous stirring at 70 °C for 4 hours to ensure complete molecular dispersion before casting. DMAC was selected as the solvent to facilitate uniform coating. Subsequently, the solution was coated onto the substrate using a doctor blade, followed by controlled solvent evaporation in an oven at 80 °C for  1 h. The overall fabrication process is illustrated in Supplementary note Fig. S1A.

Phase Composition Characterization. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy was conducted using a Spectrum 100 FTIR spectrometer (PerkinElmer) in transmission mode. Spectra (Fig.1B) were collected in the wavenumber range of 600-1500 cm-1 at room temperature to evaluate the phase composition of the PVDF films.

Raman Spectroscopy Measurement. Raman spectroscopy (Fig. 1C) was performed using a spectrometer (Horiba Jobin Yvon iHR550) coupled with a backscattering confocal microscope. A 532 nm laser was used as the excitation source. Temperature-dependent Raman spectra were collected from 25 °C to 80 °C at 7 °C intervals using a long working distance 50× objective lens (numerical aperture, NA = 0.5).

Scanning Probe Microscopy (SPM). The piezoelectric coefficient (d33) (Fig. 1D) was measured using a Cypher S atomic force microscope (AFM) equipped with conductive AC160 probes. To ensure accurate quantification and account for tip-sample contact resonance, we employed a comparative calibration method using a standard BiFeO3 thin film with a known piezoelectric

## ARTICLE IN PRESS

coefficient as a reference. A thin ITO layer (200 nm) was used as the bottom electrode to facilitate the measurement. Instead of relying solely on phase contrast, we performed local piezoelectric spectroscopy by sweeping the AC bias voltage from 1 V to 5 V. We observed a linear increase in PFM amplitude with increasing bias, confirming the film's intrinsic piezoelectric nature. By comparing the slope of the amplitude-voltage curve of our PVDF/mica heterostructure with that of the BFO reference sample, the effective d33 value was determined.

Macroscopic Piezoelectricity Measurement. The macroscopic piezoelectric response (Fig. 1F) was characterized using a single-electrode-based transparent flexible nanogenerator configuration. Wires were connected to the top and bottom electrodes of the sample, which were then linked to a low-noise current preamplifier and a low-noise voltage preamplifier to measure the output voltage. A custom-built mechanical setup was employed to repeatedly bend the samples at a frequency of 0.5 Hz, enabling evaluation of their piezoelectric performance under cyclic mechanical deformation.

Temperature-dependent XRD Measurement. Reciprocal space mapping (RSM) measurements (Fig. S3) were conducted using a Bruker D8 ADVANCE diffractometer equipped with a heater stage. A Cu Kα radiation source (λ = 0.15418 nm) and a LYNXEYE XE-T detector were employed. Compared to standard symmetric scans, asymmetric scans targeting off-axis reflections were performed to decouple the lattice expansion vectors, allowing for the independent extraction of both in-plane and out-of-plane lattice parameters.  The CTEs were derived from the linear fit of the calculated lattice strain (ΔL/L0) versus temperature. The measurements were performed over a temperature range from 30 °C to 230 °C, with data collected at 50 °C intervals. Prior to each measurement, the sample was equilibrated at the target temperature to ensure thermal stability.

Bending Curvature Measurement. The PVDF/mica heterostructures were mounted onto a custom-built stainless-steel stage, with one end clamped and the other end left free (Fig. S4A). To maintain thermal stability, the oven was preheated to the target temperature, monitored by a thermocouple to ensure the reliability of the thermal gradient. Once the set temperature was reached, the sample stage was placed in the oven, and the bending behavior of the sample was recorded. The curvature of the samples was subsequently quantified using ImageJ software by analyzing the recorded images.

Dynamic Mechanical Analysis (DMA). The elastic coefficients of PVDF and mica (Fig. S4B) were characterized using a DMA 850 system (TA Instruments) operated in a standard three-point bending configuration. Rectangular specimens with dimensions of 5 mm × 30 mm were prepared and mounted on the fixture. To ensure accurate mechanical characterization, measurements were conducted under a fixed frequency with the dynamic strain amplitude maintained strictly within the linear viscoelastic region. The temperature was ramped from -75 °C to +75 °C using a gas cooling accessory, where low-temperature nitrogen gas generated from the evaporation of liquid nitrogen was utilized to precisely control the thermal environment. The storage modulus (E') was continuously recorded as a function of temperature to quantify the mechanical stiffness evolution across the operating range.

Capacitance Measurements. Capacitance-voltage (C-V) characteristics (Fig. S5) were measured using a TF Analyzer 3000 system (AIXACCT Systems GmbH). Measurements were carried out under an applied voltage range of ±4 V DC bias with a 100 mV AC signal, sweeping across a frequency range from 1 kHz to 100 kHz.

Quantification of Pyroelectric Coefficient. The PVDF/mica, PVDF/sapphire, and pristine PVDF samples were individually mounted onto a Peltier chip (Fig. S6), which functioned as a controllable thermal source. The thickness of the sapphire is 500 μm. There is no macroscopic bending occurred during the temperature oscillation. To distinguish and accurately quantify the effective pyroelectric current, measurements were conducted using the Garn-Sharp method. A lowfrequency sinusoidal thermal stimulus (0.05 Hz) was applied using a function generator (TFG- 3605E, Twintex), and the resulting current was measured with a low-noise current preamplifier (SR570, Stanford Research Systems), starting from an initial temperature of approximately 25 °C.

Finite Element Modeling. A finite element (FE) model of the PVDF/mica bilayer was constructed using ANSYS with SOLID226 elements to simulate coupled mechanical, electrical, and thermal behaviors. Material properties were sourced from experimental measurements and tabulated data (Tables S1 and S2), considering temperature-dependent effects. Boundary conditions were applied to replicate the experimental fixation setup, with voltage-coupled nodes assigned to the PVDF surfaces. The top surface was grounded, and a 3 MΩ external resistance (CIRCU94 element) was incorporated to simulate the measurement circuit. Grounding primarily serves to establish a fixed reference potential (V = 0), which is essential for unambiguously determining the polarity of the pyroelectric response and the sign of the pyroelectric coefficient (π = dP/dT). Convective heat transfer (100 W/m2K) was applied to all outer surfaces. Simulations were performed at ambient temperatures ranging from 25 °C to 119 °C to extract curvature.
